name: Lake folk
one_line: Still water is a garden that floats: traps in the shallows, rice knocked into a canoe, and beds of mud and reed staked out on the lake itself.

needs: a lake or lagoon shore within 200 m (not the sea)
shallows for traps and beds, and a reedbed; a stream where the lagoon is brackish

staples: greens, squash and beans from the floating beds
cattail root and the reed's white base
how: fish traps and stake weirs in the shallows
spear by torchlight and line from a boat
the rice knocked into the canoe
wildfowl netted in the reeds at dusk
preserve: drying racks in the lake wind, or reed smoke
parched rice in bark boxes and pots
sugar that keeps dry all year (the maple lake)

fuel.note: cut reed dried in stooks is the lake's own fuel: quick, smoky, always there; driftwood off the shore; the shore forest adds branch and log by dressing; on a reed island the hearth sits on a flat stone so the island does not burn

shelter.form: a house on legs over the shallows, or a reed house on a reed island; walls plastered with lake clay; a boat pulled up and a rack at every door

TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.fuel: hardwood and branch from the shore wood, reed for kindling
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.food: perch and whitefish from the traps, squash and beans on the beds, maple sugar in spring
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.shelter: wattle-and-daub houses on piles along the shore, roofs of reed and bark; the canoe landing
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.palette: beech green, daub ochre, reed gold, still grey water

TAIGA.fuel: softwood and birch, driftwood; the reeds are short here
TAIGA.food: wild rice knocked into the canoe, whitefish and pike speared by torchlight, blueberries; fish frozen on the rack in winter
TAIGA.shelter: birchbark wigwams at the canoe landing, a parching pit beside the fire; in winter the ice is the road
TAIGA.palette: spruce black-green, birch white, rice gold, black water

PUNA.fuel: reed above all, tola brush from the shore; there is no tree
PUNA.food: small lake fish, duck and eggs, the reed's white base, potatoes from the shore folk
PUNA.shelter: reed houses on reed islands, rebuilt from the top as the bottom rots; reed boats; the hearth on a stone
PUNA.palette: totora gold, deep lake blue, thin high sky, straw

TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.fuel: driftwood and branch, bamboo where it grows
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.food: catfish from the traps, tomatoes and gourds on the beds, water-lily seed and lotus root
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.shelter: houses of pole and woven bamboo on stilts over the water; boats for streets
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.palette: hyacinth green, brown water, teak, egret white

FRESHWATER_MARSH.fuel: reed, and little else; a stick of driftwood
FRESHWATER_MARSH.food: eel and pike from the traps, wildfowl and eggs, cattail root; rice where the water is right
FRESHWATER_MARSH.shelter: reed houses on a hummock of reed and mud: the beginning of an island
FRESHWATER_MARSH.palette: reed gold, cattail brown, grey water, wildfowl white

LAGOON.fuel: driftwood, reed off the fresh edge
LAGOON.food: mullet and eel from the fish traps, shellfish; the beds only in the fresh corner where the stream comes in
LAGOON.shelter: stilt houses over the brackish shallows, a reed-and-driftwood weir between the piles
LAGOON.palette: seagrass green, sand, brackish grey-blue, samphire

knows: reed and cattail: the white base to eat, the stem to build, the fluff for tinder
wild rice, and the week the heads fill
willow: the stake that roots and holds a bed's edge
water lily and lotus, seed and root
the maple, and the weeks the sap runs
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the rice is knocked, never cut: what falls in the water is next year's bed; why a reed island smells of rot underneath and grows green on top
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: cattail root is bread when the traps are empty; reed cut in autumn lasts in a roof, reed cut green rots by spring; do not drink where the reedbed is still

makes: a reed boat or a bark canoe, by dressing
paddle, push pole and the rice knockers
wants_from_player: obsidian (a knife for bark and reed)

techniques.name: Floating garden
techniques.verb: stake a rectangle in the shallows, fence it with wattle, fill it with lake mud and rotting reed until it stands above the water; plant willows at the corners to root the edge
techniques.teaches: the one crop every lake gives, from the cold reed lake to the lagoon's fresh corner: nothing cleared, nothing burned, the lake bed lifted into a bed and dressed again each year with the same mud; the headman's gift because it works at every shore and is why a lake village stays under the line
techniques.unlocks: the camp's crop ceiling; a grid of beds and canals; willows in lines (ruin)

techniques.name: Wild rice
techniques.verb: two to a canoe: one poles, one bends the stalks over the gunwale and taps the grain in with a pair of sticks; then parch, tread and winnow
techniques.teaches: a crop nobody planted: half the grain falls in the water and that is next year's bed (the cold lakes only: taiga and the temperate shore)
techniques.unlocks: the camp's grain ceiling where rice grows; a store that keeps the winter

techniques.name: Line and hook
techniques.verb: twist a line, carve a hook of bone or shell, cut a pole; fish from the boat or the end of a pile
techniques.teaches: the patient way to fish; on still water the line beats the spear
techniques.unlocks: the player fishes with a pole and line

techniques.name: Drying and smoking
techniques.verb: racks in the lake wind, or over a slow reed-smoke fire
techniques.teaches: the first storage: fish keep, and so does the rice
techniques.unlocks: fish and rice keep through the lean season

techniques.name: Reed building
techniques.verb: cut reed in autumn, dry it, bind it in bundles; bundles into pillars and arches, mats for wall and floor, and a whole island laid layer on layer
techniques.teaches: a house, a floor and the ground itself from one plant, rebuilt from the top as the bottom rots
techniques.unlocks: a house of reed; a reed island on the deep lake

techniques.name: Stilt house
techniques.verb: drive poles into the lake bed, lay a platform above the flood, walls of wattle and lake clay, a roof of reed
techniques.teaches: the flood passes under the floor; the boat is the door
techniques.unlocks: a house over the water; pile stumps in the mud (ruin)

techniques.name: Birch bark
techniques.verb: peel bark in one sheet in early summer; sew boxes and a canoe with split spruce root, seal the seams with gum
techniques.teaches: a canoe light enough to carry over a portage; boxes for rice and sugar; the ember carrier's wrap (the birch lake)

techniques.name: Pottery
techniques.verb: dig clay where the lake bed shows at low water, coil a pot, fire it in a hump of clay and brush
techniques.teaches: the pot is the hinge: rice, sugar and fish oil keep in it, and on a reed island the stove sits in it
techniques.unlocks: storage; sherds in the shallows for ten thousand years (ruin)

techniques.name: Reed boat
techniques.verb: bind dry reed into two long bundles, lash them into a hull with a curved prow
techniques.teaches: a boat from the same plant as the house; it soaks, sinks slowly, and is replaced in a season or two
techniques.unlocks: cross the lake; set traps and knock rice from it (a camp craft first)

techniques.name: Fishing torch
techniques.verb: split the end of a pole and wedge in strips of birch bark (a twist of dry reed where there is no birch); stand it upright in the bow so the flame hangs out over the water
techniques.teaches: the light on the water is the lake's lamp: the fish rise to it and you see them while they cannot see you; the spear does the rest; spare bark is carried to feed it
techniques.unlocks: a torch that lights the shallows from a boat or a pile at night; fish come to the light and can be speared

wants: seed and cuttings for the beds

ladder: fire on the shore, a boat before a house
traps in the shallows: the fish_run
racks, the parching pit and the pot
rice and mats go out by water; pitch and obsidian come back
growth.restraint: traps take the shallows, never the spawning run; rice is knocked, not cut, and half of it seeds the bed; reed is cut once it has finished growing, and the island is rebuilt from the top rather than begun again; the bed takes mud from the lake and nothing from the forest
growth.ceiling_hint: a lake with a rice bed or room for beds reaches the tribal ceiling; a cold tarn with one trap stays a family

signatures.what: rows of stake stubs in the mud of the shallows, seen at low water; the mud keeps what stood on them
signatures.restore: restored: new piles driven on the old rows
signatures.inherits: the firm bar the old builders found; a house over the water in a season

signatures.what: a low mound on the shore or grounded in the shallows, a sunk reed island rotted to black earth
signatures.restore: cleared: the camp lays new reed on the old mound
signatures.inherits: the richest soil on the shore; the first bed is half built

signatures.what: rectangles of ditch in the shallows, a grid of old beds and canals, willows still standing in lines at the corners
signatures.restore: restored: the ditches cleared and the beds dressed with new mud
signatures.inherits: the beds are cut; the garden works from the first season

signatures.what: a stone-lined pit under the turf, black with old fire, beside a trodden hollow
signatures.restore: restored: the pit relined and the rice parched in it again
signatures.inherits: the rice keeps from the first harvest

signatures.what: a smooth cut in the bank where boats were dragged up, the stones raked to the sides; sometimes a boat's ribs in the mud
signatures.restore: restored: dragged clear again, a boat on it
signatures.inherits: a place to keep the boat; the boatwright comes sooner

signatures.what: sherds in the shallows and a clay pit gone to pond behind the shore
signatures.restore: cleared: the pit is dug out and the kiln hump raised beside it
signatures.inherits: the bed is clay, and the pit is already dug

ruin.plants_differ: willows in straight lines at old bed corners on a shore that otherwise grows reed; nettle and willowherb thick on a reed hummock rotting rich; a wild-rice bed that keeps itself where the folk once knocked it in

aesthetic.silhouette: a flat shore, a row of piles, houses on legs over the water; racks; the low hump of a reed island with a boat pulled up on it
sounds: rice heads rattling on the gunwale
a loon or a bittern at dusk
props: a boat pulled up, a torch pole in the bow
the parching pit and a winnowing tray
stakes and willows at a bed's edge

huts.workshop_form: a reed-and-wattle hut plastered with lake clay, set on piles at the water's edge or on the reed island, a plank walk to the door and a boat drawn up beside it
soft: reed bundles drying in stooks against the wall
a split-reed fish trap half woven on the floor
cordage hanks twisted from nettle and bark, hung on pegs
a reed mat on its frame, the weft half through
birch bark soaking in a trough
hard: a half-carved paddle held in a notched post
rice knockers in a row, one still rough
a push pole with its end being pointed
a bone hook and a shell blade on a flat stone
a bark-peeling knife of obsidian, where there is any
hearth: a clay pot of fish stew on three stones
a smoke rack of split fish over a reed fire
a parching pit and a winnowing tray
a bark torch standing ready in a pole
kiln: a hump of clay and brush, downwind
a row of coiled pots drying on a reed mat
the clay pit gone to a pond, a spade of antler beside it
huts.porch_sign: a rack of fish drying in the lake wind with a torch pole leaning at the door and a boat drawn up below
huts.library: a small reed hut on piles at the shore end of the plank walk, its shelf of rescued tomes dry above the water; the winter-count is painted on a stretched reed mat, one picture per year, with the knot-string hung beside it
third_places: the pile-house end at dusk, feet over the water

real_world.region: Lake Titicaca, Peru and Bolivia; living
real_world.note: floating islands of totora reed on a base of root blocks (khili), new reed laid on top every few weeks to months as the bottom rots; an island lasts about 25 to 30 years; houses and boats (balsas) of the same reed; fish, wildfowl and the reed's white base eaten; the stove sits on flat stones so the island does not burn; about 1,200 people on some 60 to 70 islands

real_world.region: Basin of Mexico, from c. 1100 CE; still farmed
real_world.note: rectangles staked in the shallow lake bed and fenced with wattle, filled with mud, lake sediment and rotting vegetation until above the water; ahuejote willows planted at the edges rooted them; beds about 30 x 2.5 m with canoe canals between; maize, beans, squash, amaranth, chilli and flowers, several harvests a year; a dike kept the brackish water of Texcoco off the fresh gardens

real_world.analogue: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe): manoomin, birchbark and the sugar bush
real_world.region: Great Lakes, USA and Canada; living
real_world.note: wild rice in late August: two to a canoe, one poles, one bends the stalks over the gunwale with cedar knockers and taps, and what falls in the water reseeds the bed; then parched over fire, trodden in moccasins in a lined pit, winnowed on a birchbark tray; the same bark, sewn with split spruce root and sealed with spruce gum, is the canoe, and in a split pole over the bow it is the night-spearing torch (Lac du Flambeau is named for it); from mid-March the maples are tapped into bark makakoon and about 35 gallons of sap boil to one of syrup, granulated to a sugar that keeps for months

real_world.analogue: Prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps
real_world.region: Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Slovenia, Switzerland, c. 5000 to 500 BCE
real_world.note: 111 sites of stilt houses on lake shores, rivers and wetlands, UNESCO listed; farmers and herders who fished at almost every site; the waterlogged mud kept house timbers, nets, textiles, dugouts and a wheel of c. 3400 BCE; the pile fields under the water are the ruin, and tree rings date the houses to the year

floating beds of lake-bottom weed and water hyacinth heaped with silt and staked to the bed with bamboo, rising and falling with the lake; tomatoes above all; houses of wood and woven bamboo on stilts; the fishermen row standing on one leg to see over the weed
